summary: For ages 9-10: solve multi-step number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing and rounding whole numbers up to 1,000,000. Learners apply the full place-value toolkit flexibly in context (populations, stadium capacities, distances, budgets) and tackle digit-constraint puzzles such as building the largest number with a given digit sum. The central insight is that place value drives strategy: to maximise a number you load the biggest digits into the highest-value places first. Rounding, ordering and estimation are chosen deliberately to fit each problem and checked for reasonableness.
misconceptions: Applying a memorised procedure without checking it fits.
Rounding at the wrong stage / to unhelpful accuracy.
Ordering/comparing errors with multi-zero or mixed-length numbers.
In digit-constraint puzzles, ignoring the place-value impact of digit position.

activities.title: Build the largest number: a digit-constraint puzzle
steps: Take the task: 'Make the LARGEST six-digit number whose digits add up to 15.'
Arrange digit choices into a six-column place-value chart (hundred-thousands down to ones) and write the value they build.
Compare two of their own candidate numbers place by place, starting from the highest place, and decide which is larger and why.
State the rule they discovered in their own words: to make a number as large as possible, put the biggest digits in the highest-value places first.
Verify the digits still sum to 15 after arranging them (9 + 6 = 15, then zeros gives 960,000).
activities.insight: Magnitude is controlled by the highest-value places, so maximising a number means front-loading the biggest digits into the leftmost columns while respecting the digit-sum constraint.

activities.title: Round in context for a headline
steps: Take a real-context item: 'A stadium holds 67,450 people — round it to the nearest thousand for a news headline.'
Identify the deciding digit for 'nearest thousand' (the hundreds digit) before rounding.
Place 67,450 on a number line between 67,000 and 68,000 and judge which it is nearer.
Give the rounded answer (67,000) and justify it from the deciding digit (the hundreds digit, 4), not by rounding in steps from the tens digit (67,450 → 67,500 → 68,000).
Explain in a sentence why 450 keeps the thousands the same (rounds DOWN to 67,000).
activities.insight: Rounding to a named place depends on the single deciding digit immediately to the right of that place; here the hundreds digit is 4, which is below 5, so the thousands stay the same.

activities.title: Order populations and find the range
steps: Take five city populations (mixed-length numbers, some with internal zeros) and right-align them by place-value column.
Compare from the highest place downward to order them from smallest to largest.
Order the trio 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 as a focused check, saying which place you compare first.
Find the range by subtracting the smallest from the largest and sense-check the answer against a rounded estimate.
activities.insight: Correct ordering comes from aligning place-value columns and comparing from the highest place down. For whole numbers, more digits means a larger number, but when numbers have the same number of digits you must compare place by place, not just look at the first visible digit.

activities.title: Choose and justify the strategy (think-aloud)
steps: For each problem, first answer 'which tool fits?' — number line, bar model, place-value chart, or digit arrangement — before solving.
Hear or read a worked example thought aloud, then re-solve a similar problem explaining each decision.
Estimate first by rounding, then compute the exact answer, and check the exact answer against the estimate.
Discuss with a partner or respond to prompts such as 'how did you decide?' to make the strategy deliberate.
activities.insight: In multi-step problems the hard part is choosing which place-value tool to use and checking reasonableness; making the choice explicit and estimating first turns strategy into a deliberate repertoire.

checkQuestion: Set the problem and watch the reasoning: 'Make the largest six-digit number whose digits add up to 15.' Then a context item: 'A stadium holds 67,450 people — round it to the nearest thousand for a news headline.' Watch how they place digits to maximise value and which way they round in context.
checkAnswer: 960,000 (load the biggest digits into the highest places: 9 + 6 = 15, then zeros); and 67,000 (450 is below 500, so round down).
